analysis.one_liner: Puts federal energy regulations on expiration clocks that run out unless agencies actively re-justify them.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 9 House Republican sponsors in February 2026 and referred to two committees, where it has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill tells the Department of Energy, the agencies that manage offshore drilling and federal-land mining, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to attach expiration dates to their energy regulations. Rules already in effect would be amended within 90 days to expire one year later; new rules would expire after 5 years. A rule survives only if the agency head formally extends it after taking public comment — or if the agency changes the rule in a way that has a "net deregulatory effect," which extends its life with no comment period at all. Any rule not extended simply stops being enforced and is removed from the federal rulebook.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, oil and gas producers (especially offshore drillers), coal and hardrock mining companies, and energy-intensive businesses gain the most: the safety, environmental, and efficiency rules that constrain them would face a running countdown, and an agency that fails to complete an extension process on time loses the rule entirely. The bill's sponsors frame the same result as a benefit to consumers through cheaper energy.

how_it_helps.text: Existing regulations at the Department of Energy, the federal offshore-drilling and land-management bureaus, the mining-reclamation office, and FERC would be amended within 90 days of enactment to expire no later than one year after that amendment [S2].
A covered regulation stays in force only if the agency head extends it, which requires public comment on the rule's costs and benefits and a written determination that extension is warranted [S2].
If an agency amends a rule and determines the amendment has a net deregulatory effect, the rule's expiration can be extended without any public comment process [S2].
A regulation whose expiration date passes without extension ceases to have any effect, may not be enforced, and must be removed from the Code of Federal Regulations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the downside risk: residents of communities near offshore drilling, mining, and federal energy leases would live with weakened safety and environmental oversight; consumers could face higher utility bills if Department of Energy efficiency standards lapse; and taxpayers often absorb cleanup costs, such as abandoned-mine reclamation, when industry rules are loosened. The bill itself states it creates no rights enforceable against the government, leaving people harmed by lapsed rules without a new legal remedy [S2].

drawbacks.text: The default is deletion, not review: a rule expires automatically if the agency misses the extension deadline, so long-standing safety and environmental protections — including offshore drilling safeguards written in response to the Deepwater Horizon disaster — could vanish through inaction rather than a considered decision [S2].

The easiest way to keep a rule alive is to make it weaker: an amendment judged "net deregulatory" extends the rule's life with no public comment or cost-benefit process, tilting agencies toward loosening standards [S2].

Ongoing re-justification of hundreds of rules across six agencies would consume agency resources and create regulatory uncertainty for businesses and for the public that relies on predictable standards [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does impose a real discipline — agencies must periodically defend their rules in public rather than let them sit forever. But its design makes deregulation the path of least resistance: rules die by default if not affirmatively extended, and the cheapest way to extend a rule is to weaken it. The rules targeted include offshore drilling safety standards, mining reclamation requirements, and appliance efficiency standards, so the likely costs — accident risk, pollution, cleanup liabilities, and higher energy bills — fall broadly on the public, while the savings accrue mainly to the regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees on the same day, and nothing has happened since — no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 17, 2026 by Rep. Craig Goldman of Texas with seven colleagues as cosponsors [S1][S4].

On introduction it was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee, meaning two committees would each have to act on the parts in their jurisdiction before it could reach the floor [S4].
No further action has been recorded since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost — the bill has not advanced, and current energy regulations remain in force unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; it sits in committee

for.name: 8 of 223 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Crenshaw, Pfluger, Weber, Van Duyne, Luna, Moore, Harrigan)

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors are House Republicans; no Democrat or independent has signed on, and no opponent has yet had to act because the bill has not moved.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers (offshore and federal-land drilling)
industries.note: Regulations issued under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and federal land management statutes — including offshore drilling safety and environmental rules — would face expiration clocks. Weaker or lapsed rules lower industry compliance costs while leaving accident and pollution risks with nearby communities and taxpayers.

Rules from the mining-reclamation office under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act and from land management under the Mining Law of 1872 would be subject to sunsets. Laxer reclamation and permitting rules shift cleanup and water-quality costs onto the public.

Department of Energy energy-efficiency standards for appliances fall under the bill, so those standards could lapse or be weakened. Some manufacturers gain flexibility, but constant re-litigation of standards creates planning uncertainty.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utilities and wholesale energy markets
industries.note: FERC rules governing electricity and natural gas markets would face expiration clocks. Relaxed market rules could benefit some market participants, but the uncertainty of rules that can lapse annually complicates long-term investment in reliable service.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to two committees simultaneously face a higher bar: each committee must act on its portion before the bill can reach the floor. With only 9 sponsors, no Democratic support, and no committee activity since the February referral, the realistic path is that it quietly expires at the end of this Congress, as most bills at this stage do.
